The Assam-Tibet earthquake of 1950 stands as the most
powerful earthquake ever recorded on land. With a magnitude of 8.6
on the moment magnitude scale. Its epicenter was the rugged terrain
of the Mishmi Hills in northeastern India, where the collision of the Indian plate
and the Eurasian plate unleashed seismic fury. In Tibet, the earthquake triggered colossal
landslides and extensive land cracks, dragging entire villages into rivers. India didn't fare any better. Landslides and collapse of natural dams obliterated 70 villages. Approximately 1500 people died in India, while Tibet's death toll was over 3300. And this is the mildest of the tremors
we’ll see today. That's right. We're taking a seismic journey
through history to explore some of the most powerful
earthquakes ever recorded. But before we dive in,
let's get the basics straight. Earthquakes occur
when there's a release of energy within the Earth's crust, usually caused
by the movement of tectonic plates along the fault lines. This movement generates seismic waves that spread throughout the planet,
causing the ground to shake. Today,
we'll see how these powerful vibrations can destroy entire cities
and reshape the geography of the planet. Which earthquake generated
the deadliest tsunami in history? And why didn't Earth's most powerful earthquake
kill many people? Those answers in a minute. But first,
let's make a stop in North America. In 1965, an 8.7 magnitude earthquake

originating from Rat Island
triggered a massive tsunami. With waves exceeding 10 m (33 ft)
tall, landing on Shemya Island, located 304 km (188 mi) away. Part of the Aleutian Islands in Alaska, Rat Island
earned its name when rats from a shipwreck arrived in 1780 and invaded the place. The rats were exterminated in 2008, and the island is now called Hawadax. The islands are located on the boundary
between the Pacific and North American tectonic plates, which makes it
susceptible to seismic activity. Fortunately,
since there are very few people living in this area,
the damage and casualties from this powerful
earthquake were relatively minor.

Okay,
moving on to 2010, we arrive in Chile, where an 8.8 magnitude earthquake rocked
the coast of the center of the country near the city of Concepción. Lasting approximately 3 minutes, the seismic event
caused widespread devastation with buildings
collapsing in several cities. The quake's intensity was felt across vast distances, reaching
as far as Sao Paulo, Brazil. 4620 km (2,870 mi) away. Waves as high as 15 m (50 ft)
inundated the Chilean town of Constitución, accounting for around
150 of the 525 person death toll. Tsunami warnings were issued in 53
countries, initiating preventative measures worldwide. But thankfully, the waves lost strength
before reaching the coasts of California, Hawaii, New Zealand
and Japan. Chile has a long, tumultuous history
with earthquakes, and this is not the last time
you'll see it on the list. Do earthquakes make you nervous? Well, hit that subscribe button to get
survival tips that'll keep you rock steady. Now let's venture into the remote
wilderness of Kamchatka, Russia,

confronting the seismic fury of November
5th, 1952. With a magnitude of 9.0, this earthquake rocked
the remote region of Severo-Kurilsk, situated on the Kuril Islands. Residents were alerted of a tsunami risk,
prompting them to seek safety on higher ground. However, many returned home
after the initial wave, mistakenly assuming the danger had passed. Unfortunately,
the town was hit by a second, more destructive wave
that caused even more devastation. Over 2000
people died as a result of the tsunami. Nearly half the town's population. Moving southwest, we continue with the Tohoku earthquake,
the largest ever recorded in Japan,

reaching a magnitude of 9.1. It struck on March 11th, 2011,
approximately 72 km (44 mi) off the northeast coast of Honshu,
Japan's largest island. The earthquake’s immense power
shifted Earth's axis by an estimated 10 to 25 cm (3.9 to 9.8 in), while Honshu itself moved 2.4 m (7.8 ft) eastward. And the accompanying tsunami
wave was equally devastating. When installing seawall protection around
Honshu, planners hadn't anticipated the possibility of towering waves
exceeding 40 m (130 ft). Just when you thought things couldn't
get any worse, the waves crashed into the Fukushima
nuclear power plant, triggering a meltdown
and the release of toxic nuclear waste. The disaster killed over 22,000 people. But as horrible as it was, our next earthquake
was ten times deadlier. The massive 9.1 to 9.3 magnitude earthquake
that struck Sumatra, Indonesia, in December 2004
was centuries in the making. The Burma Microplate overrode
the India tectonic plate in a geological process called subduction. The earthquake caused an astonishing uplift
of over 20 m (65 ft) on the ocean floor. The resulting tsunami
wave reaching over 30 m (98 ft) in height, devastated coastal areas in 14 countries. This natural calamity
resulted in the death of around 228,000 people. With Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Thailand experiencing
the majority of the fatalities. It continues to hold the record as the
most potent earthquake documented in Asia and is regarded
as the most catastrophic natural disaster of the 21st century. The disaster highlighted the need
for improved early warning systems and disaster preparedness measures
in vulnerable coastal communities. This next one is the second largest
earthquake ever recorded.

The great Alaska
earthquake struck on March 27th, 1964 with a magnitude of 9.2
and lasted almost 5 minutes. It occurred on the fault line,
where the Pacific plate is subducting beneath the North American plate known
as the Alaska Aleutian Subduction Zone. Anchorage, the biggest city in Alaska,
only 121 km (75 mi)  away from where the earthquake started,
got hit the hardest. Many buildings in the downtown
area were wrecked and the roads and sidewalks
sank into oblivion. The resulting tsunamis caused
widespread damage along the Pacific coast of North America, with waves
reaching California and as far as Hawaii. In total, the earthquake and its aftermath claimed the lives of 139 people, making it one of the
deadliest earthquakes in U.S. history. Our journey ends in Valdivia, Chile,

on May 22nd, 1960, where the most powerful
earthquake ever recorded rocked the planet with a magnitude of 9.5. The ten minute quake caused
several landslides across Chile's coast and rural areas, blocking roads
and making it hard for rescuers to help. After the earthquake, 25 m (82 ft) waves smashed into coastal cities,
making the destruction even worse. Hours later, tall waves
would also hit Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines,
killing hundreds of people. Despite the scale of the disaster,
Chilean citizens were alerted to the impending danger
by powerful foreshocks, which helped them prepare for the worst. Still, around 5700 people died that fateful day. The extreme power of the big earthquakes
and tsunamis we saw today has prompted scientists to develop
new safety measures. From improved early warning systems to
enhanced building codes and evacuation protocols, these advancements have helped communities
worldwide better prepare for future seismic events. It's always good to be prepared,
especially if you live in geographically unstable areas
or coastal cities. Would you recognize the signs
of an impending tsunami? Do you know the mistakes
that could cost you your life? Check out our video The worst things to do in a tsunami
right here, on How to Survive.
